insights.concise_text: The paper addresses the difficulty of sarcasm detection with traditional NLP tools and techniques by augmenting textual features with cognitive features extracted with eye-tracking.

triple.subject: cognitive features extracted with eye-tracking
triple.object: textual features used in best available sarcasm detectors

insights.concise_text: The conjecture that reading sarcastic texts induces distinctive eye movement patterns is supported by the observed average fixation duration per word being at least 1.5 times more for sarcastic texts.

triple.subject: average fixation duration per word for sarcastic texts being at least 1.5 times more than that of non-sarcastic texts
triple.object: the conjecture: Reading sarcastic texts induces distinctive eye movement patterns, compared to literal texts

insights.concise_text: Because sarcasm detection requires going beyond textual analysis, the authors train binary classifiers with cognitive features along with textual features used in best available sarcasm detectors.

triple.subject: sarcasm detection
triple.object: cognitive features along with textual features used in best available sarcasm detectors

insights.concise_text: The limitation that linguistic/stylistic features alone struggle with linguistically well-formed structures without explicit cues motivates the use of gaze-based cognition for sarcasm detection.

triple.subject: detecting sarcasm in linguistically well-formed structures, in absence of explicit cues or information (like emoticons)
triple.object: exploration of gaze-based cognition for sarcasm detection

insights.concise_text: The hypothesis that distinctive eye-movement patterns form the crux of sarcasm detection is validated using a database of 1,000 short texts, each having 10-40 words.

triple.subject: This hypothesis
triple.object: a database of 1,000 short texts, each having 10-40 words

insights.concise_text: The polarity annotation task, which did not instruct participants to annotate sarcasm, yielded accuracy of 72%-91% for sarcastic texts and 75%-91% for non-sarcastic text.

triple.subject: polarity annotation task without sarcasm instructions
triple.object: accuracy of 72%-91% for sarcastic texts and 75%-91% for non-sarcastic text

insights.concise_text: Because incorrect annotations are not discarded, the assumption that most readers identify sarcasm limits distortion of averaged eye-movement parameters for both regular and multi-instance based classifiers.

triple.subject: most of the readers, from a fairly large population, will be able to identify sarcasm
triple.object: distortion of the eye-movement parameters, averaged across all readers in our setting

insights.concise_text: The limitation that elevated average fixation duration per word may not sufficiently indicate sarcasm is addressed by combining linguistic features, readability of text and features derived from scanpaths.

triple.subject: a combination of linguistic features, readability of text and features derived from scanpaths
triple.object: elevated average fixation duration per word

insights.concise_text: Gaze, defined as simple and complex cognitive features with readability and word count features, is evaluated through stratified 10-fold cross validation on 994 examples.

triple.subject: Gaze
triple.object: 994 examples through a stratified 10-fold cross validation

insights.concise_text: The MILR classifier using the complete set of features improves over joshi2015harnessing textual sarcasm features alone, with a significant difference of p(two-tailed) = 0.02 and odds-ratio of 1.43.

triple.subject: MILR classifier with the complete set of features
triple.object: SVM classifier using only linguistic features used for sarcasm detection by joshi2015harnessing

insights.concise_text: The extended feature-set that improved the success rate of the sarcasm detector by 3.7%, over the best available system combines gaze and linguistic features, which predict correctly in sentence 4.

triple.subject: extended feature-set combining gaze and linguistic features
triple.object: the best available system by 3.7%

insights.concise_text: The system's use of cognitive features obtained from readers' eye-movement data is supported by example sentence 1, where gaze features possibly helped predict the label successfully despite textual features failing.

triple.subject: gaze features
triple.object: the sarcasm detector relying only on textual features

insights.concise_text: Only gaze features would not have sufficed to rule out other forms of incongruity that do not result in sarcasm, while the system predicts correctly when gaze and linguistic features are taken together.

triple.subject: gaze and linguistic features taken together
triple.object: the insufficiency of only gaze features

insights.concise_text: The proposed future models for learning complex gaze feature representation address information loss in the regular classification setting that may have been caused by aggregating various eye-tracking parameters.

triple.subject: models for learning complex gaze feature representation
triple.object: aggregated patterns of eye movements

insights.concise_text: The general approach of augmenting traditional linguistic features with cognitive features may be useful in other NLP sub-areas where considering textual clues alone does not prove to be sufficient.

triple.subject: augmenting traditional linguistic features with cognitive features
triple.object: other NLP sub-areas like sentiment and emotion analysis, text summarization and question answering

insights.concise_text: The extended feature-set's 3.7% improvement over the best available system is limited by errors from eye-tracker hardware, linguistic tools and resources, and possible information loss from aggregating eye-tracking parameters.

triple.subject: errors from eye-tracker hardware, linguistic tools and resources, and information loss
triple.object: the extended feature-set's 3.7% improvement

insights.concise_text: The example cases from the experiment with stratified 80%-20% train-test split include sentence 4, where gaze features alone false-indicate presence of incongruity but the combined system predicts correctly.

triple.subject: experiment with stratified 80%-20% train-test split
triple.object: sentence 4

insights.concise_text: The example cases from the experiment with stratified 80%-20% train-test split include sentence 3, a false-negative case where gaze features and the complete set of features account for erroneous prediction.

triple.subject: experiment with stratified 80%-20% train-test split
triple.object: sentence 3
